title: Notice, count, and ask
audience: Early school: grades 1 to 3, with adult reading help when necessary
intro: Start with objects, light, choices, and fair tests. These lessons prepare the ideas that later become probability, causal reasoning, and quantum science.

lessons.title: Count what you can see
lessons.objective: Count objects and compare two recorded totals.
paragraphs: A count tells you how many objects are in a group. Touch each object once as you say its number. Keep the objects still. This helps you avoid counting one object twice.
A record keeps your count after the objects move. You can draw one mark for each object. Write a name above each group. Another person can then see which count belongs to which group.
Science starts with careful records. A larger count does not explain why there are more objects. First describe what you saw. Later, you can ask what could have made the groups different.
lessons.equation: 3 + 2 = 5. Three objects and two more objects make five objects.
lessons.example: Put three red blocks and two blue blocks on a table. Count the red blocks: one, two, three. Count the blue blocks: one, two. There are five blocks in all. The red group has one more block.
lessons.exercise: Draw four circles and three squares. How many shapes are there? Which group has more shapes?
lessons.solution: There are seven shapes because four plus three equals seven. The circle group has one more shape than the square group. Count each drawing once to check.

quiz.question: Which record helps another person check a count?
options: A named group with one mark per object
quiz.explanation: The named marks connect the written count to the objects. Another person can count the marks and compare the result.

lessons.caution: A count describes this group. It does not by itself explain a cause.

lessons.title: Make clear groups
lessons.objective: Sort objects with one stated rule and explain an unclear case.
paragraphs: A group can contain objects that follow a rule. You can put all red objects together. You can also group objects by shape. State the rule before you start to sort the objects.
One object can follow two rules. A red square is red and square. If you change the rule, its group can change. The object did not change. Your question about the object changed.
An artificial intelligence system can also sort examples into groups. It needs a clear task and useful examples. A wrong group name can lead to a wrong result, even when a computer works quickly.
lessons.equation: A category is a named group. Here the rule is: colour is red.
lessons.example: Take a red square, a blue square, and a red circle. With the colour rule, two objects are red. With the shape rule, two objects are squares. Each result is correct for its own stated rule.
lessons.exercise: You have a green triangle, a green circle, and a yellow circle. Sort by colour. Then sort by shape.
lessons.solution: The colour groups contain two green objects and one yellow object. The shape groups contain one triangle and two circles. Each object belongs to one group for each rule.

quiz.question: Why can a red square appear in two different sorts?
quiz.explanation: A colour rule and a shape rule ask different questions. The same object has both properties and can satisfy both rules.

lessons.caution: Real categories can overlap. A simple sorting task does not represent every learning problem.

lessons.title: Watch a change
lessons.objective: Record a state before and after an action without adding an unsupported explanation.
paragraphs: A state describes how something is at one time. A lamp can be on or off. A cup can be empty or full. Write the time with the state when you record a change.
An action is something you do. You can press a lamp switch and then look at the lamp. Record both the action and the result. This gives more information than a record of the result alone.
Two events can happen one after the other without one causing the other. A bird can sing before a lamp comes on. That order alone does not show that the bird controls the lamp.
lessons.equation: Before: off. Action: press the switch. After: on.
lessons.example: A working battery lamp is off. You press its switch once, and it comes on. You record the starting state, your action, and the final state. Repeat with the same lamp to check whether the pattern continues.
lessons.exercise: A toy car is still. You push it, and it moves. Write a before, action, and after record.
lessons.solution: Before: the toy car is still. Action: you push the car. After: the car moves. This record states the observed sequence without claiming that all motion has the same cause.

quiz.question: What does a before-and-after record show first?
quiz.explanation: The record gives the observed states and their order. More evidence is necessary to compare causes or rule out other changes.

lessons.caution: One before-and-after record is not a controlled causal experiment.

lessons.title: Compare fairly
lessons.objective: Choose a comparison that changes one planned condition.
paragraphs: A fair comparison makes the question clear. Suppose you ask whether a steeper ramp helps a toy car travel farther. Use the same car and floor. Change the ramp height as your planned action.
Measure distance from the same starting mark each time. Release the car without an extra push. If you change the car and the ramp together, you cannot tell which change explains a different distance.
Repeat each test because small differences can occur. A wheel can turn slightly, or a floor can have a bump. Repeated results help you see whether the planned change has a stable effect.
lessons.equation: Comparison: same car, same floor, different ramp height.
lessons.example: A car travels 40 centimetres after release from a low ramp. It travels 60 centimetres from a higher ramp. You keep the car, floor, and release method the same. This is better evidence than comparing two different cars.
lessons.exercise: You test whether water helps a plant grow. Name two conditions to keep similar and one condition to change.
lessons.solution: Use similar plants, soil, light, and test times. Change the planned amount of water. Repeat with more than one plant because plants can differ even when they look similar.

quiz.question: Which ramp test gives a clearer comparison?
options: Change the ramp height and keep the car
Change the car, floor, and ramp
quiz.explanation: Keeping the car and other conditions similar makes the ramp-height change easier to study. Repetition still helps assess variation.

lessons.caution: Keeping visible conditions similar cannot guarantee that all other causes are controlled.

lessons.title: Some results are uncertain
lessons.objective: Distinguish a possible outcome from a certain outcome.
paragraphs: An outcome is a result of a trial. A trial is one try. If a closed bag holds red and blue counters, a draw can give either colour. Before the draw, the result is uncertain.

Possible means that a result can occur. Certain means that it must occur under the stated conditions. If every counter is red, a counter drawn from that bag must be red, provided the bag has not changed.

Uncertain does not mean that anything can happen. A bag with only red and blue counters cannot give a green counter under the model. State the possible outcomes before you make a prediction or run a trial.
lessons.equation: Possible outcomes: red or blue. Impossible in this bag: green.
lessons.example: A bag contains two red counters and one blue counter. You mix them and draw one without looking. Red is possible, and blue is possible. Green is not possible because no green counter is in the bag.
lessons.exercise: A bag has four yellow counters and no other counters. Is a yellow draw possible, certain, or impossible? What about blue?
lessons.solution: Yellow is certain and is therefore also possible under the stated conditions. Blue is impossible because there is no blue counter in the unchanged bag.

quiz.question: A bag contains red and blue counters. What can you claim before one unseen draw?
quiz.explanation: Both colours are present, so either can occur. The list of possible outcomes does not determine this single draw.

lessons.caution: The statement assumes that the bag contents are known and unchanged.

lessons.title: Find a pattern and test it
lessons.objective: Use a stated pattern to make a prediction and check a new case.
paragraphs: A pattern is a rule you notice in examples. The colours red, blue, red, blue suggest an alternating rule. A prediction uses that rule to say what might come next before you look at it.

A prediction can be wrong. The maker of the pattern might change the rule, or you might have guessed the wrong rule. Record the prediction first. Then compare it with a new result that you did not use.

Artificial intelligence often learns patterns from examples. A correct answer on familiar examples is not enough. New examples help test whether a system learned a useful rule or only remembered the examples it already saw.
lessons.example: You see the numbers 3, 6, and 9. You propose the rule add three and predict 12. The next hidden number is 12, so this test agrees with your rule. Other rules may still fit the first numbers.
lessons.exercise: Use the rule add four. Start at 1. Write the next three numbers, then describe how you would check your prediction.
lessons.solution: The next numbers are 5, 9, and 13. Add four at each step. Compare these predictions with new results made with the stated rule.

quiz.question: Which result gives a useful new test of a learned rule?
options: An example kept out of learning
quiz.explanation: An example kept out of learning can test a new prediction. Repeating a remembered answer does not provide the same evidence.

lessons.caution: Several rules can fit a short pattern. Agreement with one new case is not a proof.

lessons.title: Use light to ask a question
lessons.objective: Describe a light test and separate an observation from an explanation.
paragraphs: Light helps us see objects and can also be the subject of an experiment. Shine a safe lamp toward a wall. Put a card in the path. You can observe a shadow where the card blocks light.

Write what you can see before you explain it. You might record a dark region on the wall and its shape. That is an observation. A model is an explanation that tries to connect the card, lamp, and shadow.

Quantum science studies how physical systems behave, including light in carefully controlled experiments. A shadow alone does not show the full quantum rules. Later lessons use interference and measurement to examine rules that simple everyday pictures cannot capture.
lessons.equation: Test record: lamp position, card position, shadow shape.
lessons.example: Place a square card between a lamp and a wall. You observe a roughly square shadow. Move the card closer to the lamp and record the changed shadow size. Keep the lamp and wall fixed during the comparison.
lessons.exercise: A shadow grows when you move a card. Write one observation and one question for a further fair test.
lessons.solution: Observation: the recorded shadow became larger. A useful question is whether moving the card closer to the lamp increases shadow size while the lamp and wall stay fixed.

quiz.question: Which sentence is a direct observation?
options: The shadow is wider in this record
The card has a hidden wish
Every light experiment has this result
quiz.explanation: The first sentence describes the recorded appearance. The other sentences add an unsupported explanation or extend far beyond this test.

lessons.caution: Use a safe lamp. Do not look into a laser or a very bright light.

lessons.title: Store a choice with a bit
lessons.objective: Use zero and one as labels for two possible recorded states.
paragraphs: A bit is a unit of information with two possible values. We write the values as zero and one. A bit can record which of two labels applies. The labels need a stated meaning to be useful.

For a lamp record, you can let zero mean off and one mean on. This record is about the lamp. It is not the lamp itself. If someone reverses the meanings, the same written number describes a different state.

A quantum bit is called a qubit. Its rules are richer than these two labels, and later lessons explain them. Measuring a qubit in a chosen two-outcome measurement can produce a recorded bit. A qubit is not a tiny lamp.
lessons.equation: Record rule: 0 means off; 1 means on.
lessons.example: Three lamps are on, off, and on. With the stated rule, write 1, 0, 1. A reader who knows the rule can recover the recorded states. Without the rule, the numbers do not identify the lamp meanings.
lessons.exercise: Let zero mean closed and one mean open. Record three doors that are closed, closed, and open.
lessons.solution: The record is 0, 0, 1. The first two zeros mean closed, and the final one means open. State the code with the record so another reader can use it.

quiz.question: What values can one classical bit have?
quiz.explanation: A classical bit has two possible values, written zero and one. Longer messages require more bits and an agreed way to interpret them.

lessons.caution: A qubit requires quantum state rules. The lamp code is a classical information example.

lessons.title: Prediction is not control
lessons.objective: Explain why a useful clue does not necessarily cause the event it predicts.
paragraphs: A clue can help you predict an event. Dark clouds can help you predict rain. Seeing many umbrellas can also be a clue that rain is present. A useful clue need not be a control switch for the event.

Opening an umbrella does not normally make rain start. Rain can make people open umbrellas instead. To ask about a cause, ask what would change if you deliberately changed the possible cause under suitable conditions.

A prediction system can learn that umbrellas and rain occur together. A causal system must ask a further question about actions and results. Good decisions need that distinction because acting on a clue may not change the thing you want.
lessons.equation: Clue question: will it rain? Action question: what happens if I open an umbrella?
lessons.example: A child sees wet roads on rainy days and predicts rain from a wet road. A water truck can also wet a road. Making the road wet does not create rain, even though wet roads were useful clues.
lessons.exercise: Ice cream sales and swimming visits both rise on hot days. Would buying ice cream necessarily cause a person to swim? Name a possible shared cause.
lessons.solution: Buying ice cream does not necessarily cause swimming. Hot weather can increase both activities. It is a possible shared cause that must be considered before a causal claim.

quiz.question: What can make two events occur together without one causing the other?
quiz.explanation: A shared cause can affect both events. Their association can then help prediction without showing that changing one changes the other.

lessons.caution: The weather examples teach a distinction. They are not complete physical or social models.

lessons.title: Meet the three fields
lessons.objective: Separate quantum physics, causal reasoning, and artificial intelligence in one learning map.
paragraphs: Quantum physics gives rules for physical systems such as light and atoms. These rules explain experimental results that simple everyday pictures miss. We will learn their mathematics step by step instead of using the word quantum to mean mysterious.

Causal reasoning asks how actions can change results. Artificial intelligence builds systems that perform tasks such as prediction or classification. A system can predict well and still give a poor answer about the result of an action.

Quantum Causal AI is a meeting place for research questions across these fields. It is not one finished tool with a guaranteed benefit. You will first learn each field, then study carefully defined combinations and the evidence needed to evaluate them.
lessons.equation: Three questions: how does a system behave; what changes a result; what can a model learn?
lessons.example: A researcher records results from a light experiment. Quantum physics helps model the experiment. Causal reasoning helps plan which device setting to change. A learning algorithm can fit a model to records. Each part has a different job and check.
lessons.exercise: Label these tasks: predict a category from examples; compare the effect of changing a setting; model measurements of a qubit.
lessons.solution: The first task is a learning task. The second asks a causal question. The third uses quantum physics. A research project can combine them, but the labels describe different jobs.

quiz.question: Which statement is the best starting rule for this course?
options: Define each field and test each claimed combination
Every quantum model is automatically causal
A good prediction proves the cause
quiz.explanation: Clear definitions keep the three tasks distinct. Each proposed combination needs its own assumptions, measurements, and evidence for the claimed result.

lessons.caution: This is a study path. It does not claim a general quantum advantage for causal learning.
